lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6 you gave feedback. What does 'Even better if' give? (One thing to improve next time.) Today: how to lead a group fairly, as a referee, a captain or a coach.
A referee (or umpire) applies the rules fairly. Good officials know the rules and keep in a place where they can see. They decide quickly, signal clearly, stay calm, and treat both teams the same.

Football's signals (the Laws of the Game): advantage, both arms forward; a direct free kick, an arm pointing the way; an indirect free kick, an arm straight up until another player touches the ball; a penalty, pointing at the spot.

Advantage: if a team is fouled but still has a good chance, the referee lets play go on. Then the foul does not help the team that did it. If the chance is gone within a few seconds, the free kick is given after all.

A captain leads on the field: encourages teammates, speaks calmly with the referee, sets an example of fair play, and shakes hands at the end, win or lose. A good captain lifts the team after a mistake.

A coach plans practices and gives feedback. Keep it short and specific, one point at a time, with what went well first: 'Great run! Next time, look up before you pass' helps far more than 'That was bad.'
A tournament: in a knockout, losers go out, so 8 teams play 8 − 1 = 7 matches. In a round robin, everyone plays everyone: 4 teams play 4 × 3 ÷ 2 = 6 matches.
Try it in the world: run a mini tournament in your world for friends, with a board of matches and results. For real: referee a short game at school and use the signals. Next: sleep for teenagers.

exercises.hint: Look at the raised arm: held straight up, high.
exercises.explain: An arm raised straight up: an indirect free kick, so a goal only counts after another player touches it.

exercises.prompt: A good referee changes decisions to please whoever shouts loudest.
exercises.hint: What makes an official fair to both teams?
exercises.explain: False: a fair referee decides by the rules, calmly, whoever shouts.

exercises.prompt: Who leads a team on the field and speaks with the referee?
exercises.hint: Which player often wears an armband?
exercises.explain: The captain leads on the field and speaks calmly with the referee.

exercises.prompt: A knockout has 16 teams. How many matches are needed to find a winner?
exercises.hint: Every team except the winner loses exactly once.

exercises.prompt: Match each role to its job.
exercises.hint: Who is on the field, who is beside it, and who is in charge of the rules?
exercises.explain: Referee: the rules. Captain: leads on the field. Coach: practices and feedback. Timekeeper: the clock.

exercises.prompt: In a round robin, every team plays every other once. How many matches do 5 teams play?
exercises.hint: Each team plays the 4 others; then halve, because each match has two teams.

exercises.prompt: Mimi is fouled but passes to Zara, who is clear through on goal. What should the referee do?
exercises.hint: Would stopping play help the team that did the foul?
exercises.explain: Advantage: stopping play would take away Zara's chance, so play goes on.

items: give one clear thing to improve
exercises.hint: Start positive, then one point, how, practice, praise.
exercises.explain: What went well, one thing to improve, how to do it, a new try, and praise for the effort.

items: owning up to a last touch
exercises.hint: Would you be happy if the other team did it to you?
exercises.explain: Fair play: shaking hands, helping an opponent up, owning up. Not: arguing every decision, pretending.

exercises.prompt: In a round robin, every team plays every other team once.
exercises.hint: Think of the name: the matches go all the way round.
Both arms are stretched forward, the way the team is attacking.
exercises.explain: Both arms forward: advantage. Play goes on because the fouled team still has a good chance.

exercises.prompt: A round robin of 6 teams on 3 pitches, 10 minutes a match. How many minutes does it take at least?
exercises.hint: Find the matches, then the rounds the pitches need, then the time.
exercises.explain: 6 × 5 ÷ 2 = 15 matches; 3 pitches play 3 at once, so 5 rounds; 5 × 10 = 50 minutes.

exercises.prompt: A teammate keeps passing too late. Which feedback helps most?
choices: Look up early and pass before the tackle.
exercises.hint: Good feedback is specific: it says what to do next time.
exercises.explain: 'Look up early and pass before the tackle': one clear thing, and how.

exercises.prompt: If the advantage does not lead to a chance within a few seconds, the referee can still give the free kick.
exercises.hint: Advantage should never help the team that did the foul.
exercises.explain: True: if the advantage does not happen, the referee goes back and gives the free kick.

exercises.prompt: You are refereeing a friendly. Your brother's team trips an attacker in their penalty area. What do you give?
choices: a penalty kick, as for any team
exercises.hint: A referee treats both teams the same.
exercises.explain: A penalty kick: a foul in the penalty area, whoever the players are.

exercises.prompt: 8 teams play a round robin, then the top 4 play a knockout. How many matches in all?
exercises.hint: Round robin: 8 × 7 ÷ 2. Knockout of 4: one fewer than the teams.

exercises.prompt: Put a referee's steps for advantage in order.
items: give the free kick if the chance is lost
check if the team still has a chance
exercises.explain: See the foul, judge the chance, signal and call 'Play on!', watch, and give the free kick if the chance goes.
